The Monty Hall Problem

CountingLogicGame Strategy
Game: A car is hidden behind one of three doors and goats are behind the other two. Pick a door and see what you would win if you stayed with it and what you would win if you switched.
How to play: Press a door. The doors open to show what was behind each, and the table counts how often staying and switching would have won. Press a door again for the next round.

Look for the math

The page below the game quotes a reader who says that once the host opens a goat door, "two doors remain with a 50-50 chance". That is the common mistake. What the host's opening tells you depends on how the host chooses the door, and in the usual game the two doors are not equally likely.

Count the nine cases

Call the doors 1, 2 and 3. There are 3 places for the car and 3 first picks, 9 equally likely cases. If your first pick is the car (3 cases), the host opens one of two goat doors, and staying wins. If your first pick is a goat (6 cases), the host has only one door he can open, and the car is behind the other closed door, so switching wins. So staying wins in 3 of 9 cases (1/3) and switching in 6 of 9 (2/3). The counters above are filled in this way: whatever door you press, a goat door means switching would have won. The test counted all nine cases, and a simulation of 600,000 rounds gave 33.4% and 66.6%.

The host's mindset

The reader is right that the host's behaviour matters. If a host opens one of the other two doors at random, and it happens to show a goat, then staying and switching really are 1/2 each (the test counts 6 of 12 for each). If a host opens a door only when you picked the car, switching always loses; if he opens one only when you picked a goat, switching always wins. The game's classic version, a host who knows where the car is and always opens a goat door, gives 1/3 and 2/3.

More doors

With 100 doors, you pick one and the host opens 98 goat doors, the unlucky door you left is almost surely the car: switching wins 99 times in 100. The same counting works for any number of doors: staying wins once in N, switching wins N−1 times in N.

Press Play 100 rounds a few times. Does the share of "switched and won" settle near two thirds? What would you expect after 1,000 rounds?
